summary: Describes how ISI implemented the Mail Transfer Protocol on TOPS-20 machines, supporting both sender and receiver roles over TCP and NCP. Mail is queued in files and a background program dispatches it.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a builder's notebook showing how one team made a mail-delivery program work on one kind of computer, with a queue that sends mail in the background.

questions: how mail was delivered on tops-20
how was mail routed during protocol transition
subtitle: How ISI built a mail system for TOPS-20 using the new Internet protocols.

tldr.problem: ISI needed a working Mail Transfer Protocol implementation on TOPS-20 machines that could handle both the old ARPANET protocols and the new Internet protocols during the transition period.
tldr.mechanism: ISI built separate receiver and sender programs for MTP over both TCP and NCP, with a background dispatcher that processes mail from multiple sources and routes it to the appropriate output channel based on destination capabilities.
tldr.outcome: The implementation allows mail to flow between old and new protocol systems. Mail is stored in two-file format (control file and data file) so delivery status can be updated as mail is processed.

today: RFC 784 documents the ISI implementation of MTP for a specific platform during the ARPANET to Internet transition. TOPS-20 systems are now historical, and the transition to Internet protocols is complete.

sections.title: Building a Transition Mail System
sections.content:
ISI created an implementation of the Mail Transfer Protocol for TOPS-20 machines (written in BLISS-10), supporting both TCP and NCP as transport services. The system provides both MTP sender and MTP receiver functions, bridging mail between hosts using old ARPANET protocols and hosts using new Internet protocols.

The implementation includes interfaces to other mail delivery mechanisms and tables indicating for each host whether it can accept mail via MTP on TCP, MTP on NCP, or FTP on NCP (the traditional method).
sections.plainLanguage: ISI built a mail post office on TOPS-20 computers that could accept packages from both old and new delivery systems.

sections.title: Mail Flow Architecture
sections.content:
Mail sources (user composition programs like Hermes and MM, or system mail receivers from various channels) create mail files in user directories. A background dispatcher program processes these files and routes them to appropriate output channels. Users can also invoke a synchronous version to send mail immediately if a channel is available.

Mail is stored in a two-file format: a control file containing delivery information and a pointer, plus a data file containing the RFC 733 message header and body. This design allows the control information to be modified as mail is processed (marking recipients as sent, retrying failed recipients) while the message data is only read.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail files sit in a queue. A program wakes up regularly, looks at the queue, and tries to deliver each piece to the right place. It keeps track of what worked and what didn't.

sections.title: Components and Tables
sections.content:
The system consists of five main components: MTP receivers for TCP and NCP, a dispatcher, and MTP senders for TCP and NCP. Additionally, it uses a Host Mail Capability table that specifies for each destination host which channels can deliver mail to it (MTP on TCP, MTP on NCP, or old FTP on NCP), and a Host special processing table for routing to systems outside the standard protocols (for example, hosts in England via UCL's mail system).

Mail composition programs interface with the existing user mailbox file system. Other mail sources and sinks can be integrated as requested.
sections.plainLanguage: Different routers for TCP and NCP move mail along. Tables say which routers can reach which destinations. The whole system fits together so nothing breaks.

references.text: Crocker, D., et al., "Standard for the Format of ARPA Network Text Messages," RFC 733, November 1977.
